mainText:
If you only remember one thing: the people building A I are now openly talking about slowing it down. Anthropic's C E O Dario Amodei published an essay arguing labs should deliberately pace capability gains so safety can catch up, and rivals across the industry are agreeing with him. The White House is not.

Story one. A I development: pacing the frontier.

Amodei's essay warns that A I is now accelerating its own development, and that within six to twelve months, a swarm of A I agents could be capable of taking over large parts of the internet. His fix: embed third party evaluators inside labs, build shared safety standards among democratic countries' labs, and coordinate carefully with authoritarian regimes.

Sam Altman committed to third party evaluators. Elon Musk said, quote, Dario is right, unquote. Demis Hassabis and Microsoft's Satya Nadella backed the direction too.

President Trump dismissed the slowdown push, calling its advocates, quote, very negative forces, unquote, pushing things that won't happen, and argued the U S should keep racing since whoever wins A I wins.

From your Reads: Tech Policy Press is asking the sharper question behind the headlines, who actually sets the pace, flagging that pacing might be about commercial advantage as much as safety.

Why it matters: unreleased frontier models may be showing capability jumps big enough to spook their own builders, but slowing down means very different things to safety researchers, open source advocates, and a White House betting on A I dominance.

Story two. A I ethics and safety.

Anthropic says it disrupted campaigns by three Chinese A I labs that allegedly routed millions of queries through Claude to harvest training data and distill it into their own models. U S officials are calling it industrial scale theft, just two weeks before Trump and Xi are due to meet. Beijing rejected the claims and warned of retaliation. That's from your Reads, the China A I Weekly Digest.

Twenty five Fields Medalists signed a declaration warning that A I's race to solve math problems is sacrificing mathematical understanding and proper attribution, the human process that actually advances the field. That's from The Rundown.

Two A I safety researchers, at Anthropic and Google DeepMind, resigned to join the independent evaluator METR, both citing concerns that capabilities are outpacing safety work.

Why it matters: the safety conversation isn't just blog posts anymore, it's showing up in resignations, I P disputes, and warnings from math's most prestigious prize.

Story three. Tech geopolitics.

DeepSeek shipped a new model called V four point one Flash, five hundred fifty two billion parameters, that reportedly beat both OpenAI's G P T five point six Sol and Moonshot's Kimi K three on coding and agentic tasks, while the company quietly lines up a Shanghai listing at roughly a seventy four billion dollar valuation.

China's chip I P O wave crested with Enflame, a Tencent backed Nvidia challenger, debuting up one hundred eighty eight percent on Shanghai's STAR market, valuing it near twenty five and a half billion dollars. It's the last of China's, quote, four A I chip dragons, unquote, to go public.

Meanwhile, Washington has quietly eased up. The Commerce Department shifted to case by case licensing for advanced chip exports to China, with volume caps and a twenty five percent tariff, as the White House prioritizes stable trade talks ahead of Trump's Beijing visit.

South Korea is toughening its espionage law specifically to protect chip secrets from China, and Nikkei reports the U S will press China on A I linked cyberattacks at the September twenty fourth Trump Xi summit.

Why it matters: chip policy and A I diplomacy are now openly tangled up with the Trump Xi meeting, expect more swings between confrontation and dealmaking through the end of the month.

Story four. A I industry and business.

Anthropic told investors it expects to turn profitable next quarter, with gross margins above eighty percent and eleven and a half billion dollars in revenue.

Tech layoffs have already crossed six thousand three hundred in the first ten days of September, led by Uber's roughly three thousand three hundred role corporate cut, about ten percent of its workforce.

And from your Reads, The Information: a very on brand comms disaster. That's the top of the news. Your full briefing is in the recording.
